title: Here are 5 of the most haunted locations you can visit in Louisville
excerpt: Discover the chilling ghost stories and unexplained activity haunting these five historic Louisville landmarks, including the Waverly Hills Sanatorium.
content:
Oct. 21, 2026, 5:01 a.m. ET

  • Several historic Louisville venues, including theaters and hotels, are reportedly home to paranormal activity.
  • The Brown Theatre is said to be haunted by the ghosts of two lovers who died tragically at the venue.
  • Multiple spirits, including a former engineer and a "Lady in Gray," have been reported at the Louisville Palace.
  • Waverly Hills Sanatorium, a former tuberculosis hospital, is considered one of the most haunted places in the world.
  • Staff and guests at Pizza Lupo and The Seelbach Hilton have also reported unexplained events and ghostly sightings.

Have you ever seen something that a second later wasn't there? Or maybe you saw an object inexplicably move across a room or heard the sound of children's laughter?

If so, you might have visited one of these five haunted locations in Louisville. Several historic venues, including The Brown Hotel, Pizza Lupo and the Waverly Hills Sanatorium, are reportedly home to paranormal activity.

Just in time for Halloween, discover the chilling ghost stories and unexplained activity haunting these five historic Louisville landmarks:

5 of the most haunted places in Louisville

The Brown Theatre

Details: 315 W. Broadway, Louisville, Ky., kentuckyperformingarts.org

The Brown Theatre, which celebrated 100 years in 2025, has a long history as a playhouse, movie theater and vibrant space for the arts in downtown Louisville. The historic venue seats 1,443 patrons and according to those that work there, it is also home to a pair of star-crossed lovers who haunt the theater, which is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

According to a history of the Brown Theatre written by Clyde Luther, "an actress and a theatre employee fell in love during an ill-fated affair. But the love affair was not to be, the theater employee was already married. The girl either hanged herself on a spiral staircase backstage or fell to her death. The distraught fellow (died by suicide)."

Luther continues, saying "the lovers have been seen at night in the theater. She in a flowing white gown standing on the stage, right loft. He, in tails and formal attire on the stage, gazing up at his lover. He has also been seen wandering the lobby. They are dressed for their wedding, which never took place."

Late at night, stagehands have reported footsteps directly above them when no one else should have been in the building. There are also reports of an apparition standing near the theater's loading door at night.

"I have not seen the ghosts myself," Will Richards, manager of the Brown Theatre, previously told The Courier Journal. "But we had a father and son who cleaned the theater at night. On one occasion, when the theater was empty, the son looked up from main floor where he was cleaning and saw a lady in white on the balcony. When he looked again, she was gone. He ran out the front door of the theater and did not come back."

Louisville Palace

Details: 625 S. Fourth St., Louisville, Ky., louisvillepalace.com

The Louisville Palace, which first opened in 1928, has attracted several spirits throughout its nearly 100 year history.

The most well-known spirit is that of Fred Frisch, who was the theater's longtime chief engineer. Frisch had a heart attack and died in the downstairs maintenance room on Oct. 27, 1965, The Courier Journal previously reported. Over the years, several staff members have reported seeing an apparition of an older male in a plaid shirt with a flat top and thick, black-rimmed glasses, a description that resembles a photo of Frisch that Frisch’s grandson gifted to the theater, which now hangs in the downstairs catering room.

According to staff, Frisch tends to appear or make himself known when the building, or someone, in it is in trouble. A few years ago, the Palace's general manager Johnny Downs was closing up the theater when every light began to flicker, something he said didn’t make sense because many of those lights were on different circuits. So, Downs headed backstage to check the electricity, and realized a pipe was leaking. Once he fixed the pipe, the lights stopped flickering. If that water had run overnight, it would have flooded the back part of the theater, The Courier Journal previously reported.

The Palace is also home to "The Lady in Gray,” a residual spirit who wears a high-collared 1940s-era dress, holds a program for a show and has her hair in a bun. She's either seen walking up the stairs near the Palace’s entrance or coming down one of the aisles in the theater itself. She usually takes about five steps and then disappears, The Courier Journal previously reported.

A third spirit has also been spotted in the theater near the stairway that leads to what used to be a gentlemen’s lounge, where men would smoke. Decades later, staff say the spirit brings about the scent of a freshly-smoked cigar.

Other encounters include women working in the production area who have reported feeling someone tug their ponytails, only to discover no one is there. Staff has also reported hearing mysterious child-like laughter, and Downs has two theories about who those kids might be. In the late 1800s, a tornado blew through downtown Louisville, and wiped out what used to be a hospital as well as the original site of St. Joseph’s Children’s Home. There’s also a part of the theater near the main floor bar area that was once part of a music store, and that business offered music lessons to children, The Courier Journal previously reported.

Pizza Lupo

Details: 1540 Frankfort Ave., Louisville, Ky., pizzalupo.com

Pizza Lupo, one of Louisville's favorite pizzerias, serves the popular "Sting Like a Bee" pie, with a side of spooky sensations.

In the basement of Pizza Lupo, 1540 Frankfort Ave., solid items have been known to fly off shelves and mimics of servers' voices, sneezes and hiccups can sometimes be heard. There is an old well in the basement that leads to the original Louisville cistern and a child's doll sits at the bottom, The Courier Journal previously reported.

Owner Max Balliet opened Pizza Lupo in the 150-year-old building in 2017 and previously told The Courier Journal that he's lost count of how many unexplainable occurrences have happened there.

In 2020, then-server Katie Day told The Courier Journal she was "violently shoved" between the shoulder blades. When she turned around, no one was there.

Day also recounted one evening when a huge rumble shook the whole building, causing dust and dirt from the brick of the old building to fall all over the restaurant.

"It sounded like a 300-pound something belly-flopped on the floor upstairs, and it was during service," Balliet said at the time. "I went up there and opened the locked office, expecting to see an entire shelf fallen on the floor, and there was literally no sign of anything out of place. But something happened in that room to create such a violent bang it shook dust loose."

The Seelbach Hilton

Details: 500 S. Fourth St., Louisville, Ky; seelbachhilton.com

The Seelbach Hotel in downtown Louisville was founded by Bavarian-born immigrant brothers Louis and Otto Seelbach and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. During its years downtown, many guests have reported strange sounds and activity during their stays, including sightings of the mysterious “Lady in Blue." Legend says she was there to meet her husband at the hotel, but he was killed in an accident and the widow then either jumped or fell down an elevator shaft, The Courier Journal previously reported.

There have also been reports of televisions turning on at a loud volume early in the morning and the sound of running footsteps on wooden floors.

"The building is very haunted," night security guard Patrick Rhodes previously told The Courier Journal. "Between Al Capone and the gangsters (staying here), World War I and II and the Great Depression and the age of the building, there's lots of different things that have happened here."

The Seelbach's ghost lore has been well documented, and U.S. News & World Report featured the hotel in a story titled "The 27 most haunted hotels in America," which also states "some hotel guests today say they've felt cold spots or caught the unexplained aroma of perfume during their stay."

People regularly visit The Seelbach specifically to experience its supernatural energy. Mediums, ghost hunters, and witches have all visited and asked Rhodes to take them on a late-night ghost tour.

"I've heard doctors, lawyers, construction people, grandmothers, everybody in every realm that have reported doors opening and closing, lights flickering on and off, or the smell of perfume," Rhodes previously said of the infamous "Lady in Blue." "Maybe a blue streak of light going across a room. I have thousands and I'm still adding to the stories."

Waverly Hills Sanatorium

Details: 4400 Paralee Drive, Louisville, Ky.; therealwaverlyhills.com

In the early 1900s, Jefferson County was ravaged by an outbreak of tuberculosis which prompted the construction of a The Waverly Hills Sanatorium. The two-story facility opened in 1910 and was able to accommodate between 40 and 50 tuberculosis patients, according to the Waverly Hill Sanatorium website.

The tuberculosis hospital closed in 1961 and reopened in 1962 as Wood Haven Medical Services, a geriatric facility. Woodhaven had numerous complaints over patient neglect and was closed by the state in 1982.

After closing, Waverly Hills gained a reputation as one of the world’s most haunted places. Prior to designation on the National Register of Historic Places, Waverly Hills had been left to decay. The abandoned hospital gained notoriety as a popular ghost hunting spot for local teens and lovers of the paranormal.

In 2001, Charles and Tina Mattingly purchased the property and began its restoration, according to the Waverly Hill Sanatorium website. Many working on the building's restoration reported unexplained slamming doors and sightings of a mysterious man in white drifting throughout the corridors. Others had run-ins with Timmy, a spectral boy who roams the hallways and likes to play ball, the website states, adding that when the facility officially opened to the public for tours, visitors continued to corroborate these experiences.

"Once you went to Waverly Hills, you became a permanent resident," the Waverly Hills Historical Society states on its website.

Waverly Hills attracts tourists from around the country who can take paranormal and historical guided tours. It also allows private paranormal groups to host investigations of the facility, many of whom claim to have experienced inexplicable paranormal activity during their visits. Waverly Hills has been featured on ABC/FOX Family channel's "Scariest Places on Earth," VH1's"Celebrity Paranormal Project," Syfy's "Ghost Hunters," and HuLu's "Living for the Dead."

Reporters Kirby Adams and Gege Reed contributed to this report. Reach Courier-Journal reporter Maggie Menderski at mmenderski@courier-journal.com.
